paragraphs: Recognizing sound events becomes harder when training labels are weak or noisy. The paper argues that, in these adverse conditions, a single learning stage is insufficient. It proposes sequential self-teaching: a stage-by-stage learning process intended to improve how well a sound recognition system generalizes beyond its training examples.

The contribution centers on the learning process applied to a modeling system. Its motivation is that difficult supervision calls for successive stages of learning. The authors support this approach with technical results and evaluate it on Audioset, where they report performance improvements of up to 9%. That figure describes the improvement the method can achieve in the reported evaluation, rather than a guaranteed gain for every sound recognition task.

The evaluation also examines transfer learning, where knowledge from a previously trained model is used for another task. The authors find that sequential learning improves the transferability of that knowledge. Together, the findings support the approach as a way to improve both sound recognition performance and generalization when reusing trained models.
icml-2020-a-sequential-self-teaching-app.tldr: Sequential self-teaching improves sound recognition and knowledge transfer, with reported performance gains of up to 9% on Audioset.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned account of how the environment changes to support decision making. A forward dynamics model predicts what comes next, but inaccurate predictions can seriously undermine the resulting policy. This paper investigates whether adding a backward dynamics model can reduce dependence on the forward model's accuracy.

The proposed method, Bidirectional Model-based Policy Optimization, uses both models to generate short, branched rollouts for policy optimization. These rollouts supply simulated experience from dynamics modeled in both directions. The central change is therefore how experience is generated for learning: the policy no longer relies exclusively on predictions from a single forward model.

The authors derive a tighter bound on return discrepancy, providing theoretical support for the bidirectional approach compared with using only the forward model. Their experiments also report better sample efficiency and asymptotic performance than the model-based methods used for comparison. These results indicate benefits both in how efficiently the method learns from experience and in the performance it reaches after continued learning.
icml-2020-bidirectional-model-based-poli.tldr: BMPO combines forward and backward dynamics models to improve policy learning, supported by a tighter return-discrepancy bound and empirical performance gains.

paragraphs: Causal identification asks whether the effect of an intervention can be determined from available distributions together with assumptions expressed in a causal graph. This paper addresses a practical complication: different studies may measure different sets of variables. The evidence available across studies therefore need not cover every modeled variable consistently.

The authors study how the factors making up a causal effect relate to identification when observations are incomplete in this sense. They examine these factors at different levels of abstraction and characterize relationships relevant to a particular intervention. This analysis provides the basis for a graphical criterion that is sufficient to establish identification from partially observed distributions.

Building on those graphical properties, the paper develops an algorithm that returns an expression for a causal effect using the available distributions. The contribution connects a theoretical identification condition to a usable formula. Because the stated criterion is sufficient, satisfying it establishes identifiability; the abstract does not claim that failing it proves identification impossible.
icml-2020-causal-effect-identifiability-.tldr: The paper gives a sufficient graphical criterion and an algorithm for identifying causal effects from distributions that observe different variable sets.

paragraphs: Overestimation bias occurs when a learning system assigns overly optimistic values to its choices. The paper treats this as a major obstacle to accurate off-policy reinforcement learning and studies how to reduce it in continuous control. Its proposed method is Truncated Quantile Critics, abbreviated TQC.

TQC combines three components: a distributional representation of each critic's predictions, truncation of those predictions, and an ensemble of multiple critics. Representing predictions as a distribution gives the method more structure to adjust than a single value estimate. Together, distributional representation and truncation allow finely adjustable control over overestimation. The ensemble supplies an additional improvement in the reported scores.

The authors report that TQC exceeds the state of the art on every environment in the continuous control benchmark suite they evaluate. On Humanoid, described as the most challenging environment, the reported improvement is 25%. These findings connect the method's explicit control of optimistic value estimates with stronger empirical control performance across the evaluated suite.
icml-2020-controlling-overestimation-bia.tldr: TQC combines distributional critics, prediction truncation, and ensembling to control overestimation and improve continuous control benchmark performance.

paragraphs: CURL addresses reinforcement learning directly from images. Its approach extracts higher-level features from raw pixels through contrastive learning, then performs off-policy control using those features. This connects visual representation learning with the task of learning which actions to take.

The distinction between pixels and state-based features is central to the reported results. An image-based method must learn useful features from visual observations, whereas a state-based method receives features describing the state. CURL nearly matches the sample efficiency of state-based methods on the DeepMind Control Suite. The authors describe it as the first image-based algorithm to achieve that near match on this suite.

The paper also compares CURL with earlier pixel-based approaches, including both model-based and model-free methods. It reports performance gains of 1.9 times on the DeepMind Control Suite and 1.2 times on Atari at the respective 100,000-step benchmarks. These findings support contrastive feature learning as a useful component for control from pixels when the amount of environment interaction is limited.
icml-2020-curl-contrastive-unsupervised-.tldr: CURL learns contrastive visual features for off-policy control, improving pixel-based benchmarks and nearly matching state-based sample efficiency on the DeepMind Control Suite.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing can provide certificates that a model withstands bounded adversarial perturbations. Gaussian smoothing already offers useful guarantees for perturbations measured with the l2 norm. This paper asks how well smoothing can extend to other norms, particularly when the input has many dimensions.

For a broad class of independent, identically distributed smoothing distributions, the authors prove that the largest certifiable lp radius scales no better than O(1/d^(1/2 − 1/p)) for p greater than 2. Here, d is input dimension. The certificate therefore shrinks as dimension increases. For p at least 2, the dimension dependence does not improve on isotropic Gaussian smoothing.

Within generalized Gaussian smoothing, the relevant bounds asymptotically agree up to a constant factor, making Gaussian smoothing optimal to that precision. The paper also gives worse dimension-dependent upper bounds for uniform smoothing within l1 and l-infinity balls. Experiments on CIFAR support the theory. The result identifies limits on the certificates obtainable through these smoothing families, rather than claiming that every robustness approach faces the same restriction.
icml-2020-curse-of-dimensionality-on-ran.tldr: For broad smoothing families, certifiable robustness under lp perturbations with p greater than 2 deteriorates with dimension and cannot improve on Gaussian dimension scaling.

paragraphs: Operator-valued kernels extend kernel learning to outputs that belong to a Hilbert space, including infinite-dimensional outputs. This makes the framework relevant to functional regression and structured prediction. However, the computational reliance on an output-space kernel trick has led much previous work to use squared-norm loss, leaving robustness concerns insufficiently addressed.

The paper develops a duality approach that permits a wider range of losses in these models. A central difficulty is that the dual optimization involves infinite-dimensional Lagrange multipliers. The authors handle them through a Double Representer Theorem, providing the mathematical basis for solving the resulting learning problems.

They give detailed algorithms for epsilon-insensitive losses and the Huber loss, extending the usable loss choices beyond squared error. A theoretical stability analysis supports the robustness benefits, and experiments show improvements on structured-data applications. The contribution is both a broader optimization framework and evidence that this flexibility can make structured-output kernel learning more robust in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-duality-in-rkhss-with-infinite.tldr: A duality framework enables robust losses for operator-valued kernel models with infinite-dimensional outputs, with theoretical stability and empirical benefits.

paragraphs: The paper studies identification in linear causal models: determining structural coefficients within a model of causal relationships. These coefficients describe the relationships specified by the linear system. The central contribution is an identification algorithm whose running time is polynomial, making computational efficiency part of the result.

The algorithm subsumes earlier efficient state-of-the-art methods and brings together several previously separate approaches. Subsuming those methods means its identification capabilities encompass what those methods could handle. Unification matters because it places multiple approaches within a shared procedure. This is a claim about the reach of an efficient identification method within linear causal models, rather than a claim that every coefficient in every model is identifiable.

The authors then build on this result to develop a procedure for identifying total causal effects in linear systems. This extends the focus from individual structural coefficients to the overall effects represented by the system. The paper thus links efficient coefficient identification with a procedure addressing a broader causal quantity.
icml-2020-efficient-identification-in-li.tldr: The paper unifies earlier efficient identification methods in a polynomial-time algorithm for linear causal models and develops a procedure for total causal effects.

paragraphs: The paper establishes two useful properties of the 1-path-norm for shallow neural networks. The first concerns optimization: despite being non-smooth and non-convex, this regularizer has a closed-form proximal operator that can be computed efficiently. That operator provides a way to incorporate the regularizer into a learning update.

This result enables stochastic proximal-gradient-type methods for regularized empirical risk minimization. The second property concerns sensitivity to input changes. When the network's activation function is differentiable, the 1-path-norm bounds the network's Lipschitz constant. The authors show that this bound is tighter than the straightforward product of layer-level Lipschitz bounds, motivating its use in training against adversarial perturbations.

Experiments illustrate the advantages of the proximal mapping and compare the robustness–accuracy tradeoff from three approaches: the 1-path-norm, L1 regularization, and layer-wise Lipschitz constraints used in Parseval networks. The contribution therefore joins an efficient optimization tool with a theoretical reason to study the same regularizer for robustness; the abstract does not declare a universal winner in the empirical comparison.
icml-2020-efficient-proximal-mapping-of-.tldr: The 1-path-norm admits an efficient proximal operator and, with differentiable activations, a tighter network sensitivity bound that motivates robustness applications.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a compact representation of uncertainty about a deep neural network's parameters. It approximates the parameter posterior with a multivariate normal distribution, expressed in information form. In this representation, the information matrix is the inverse of the covariance matrix.

The key observation is that the information matrix tends to have a sparse spectrum. This is a statement about its spectral structure, which makes dimensionality reduction through low-rank approximations useful. The authors develop a sparsification algorithm to exploit that structure and derive an analytical sampler designed to be computationally economical. Representation and sampling are therefore addressed together.

The resulting method makes information-form uncertainty representation scalable for deep networks. The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and evaluations across several benchmarks, reporting competitiveness with existing methods. Its significance is the use of structure in the inverse covariance to make a parameter-posterior approximation more manageable, while retaining a practical way to sample from the uncertainty representation.
icml-2020-estimating-model-uncertainty-o.tldr: The method exploits spectral sparsity in an inverse-covariance representation to estimate and sample neural-network parameter uncertainty efficiently.

paragraphs: This paper studies faster neural-network inference through sparse activation maps. ReLU activations naturally produce zeros in many settings, creating an opportunity to reduce computation. The authors investigate both how to increase this sparsity in a trained network and how to turn it into actual execution speed.

To make activation maps sparser, they introduce a regularization technique together with threshold-based sparsification using a parameterized activation called FATReLU. Their image-classification experiments show that most architectures examined can accommodate substantially sparser activations without losing accuracy. This finding concerns the tested architectures rather than an unconditional property of every network.

Sparse activations only yield practical benefits if the computation can exploit them. The paper therefore also introduces an algorithm for fast convolution with sparse inputs. On a range of popular ImageNet models running on modern Intel CPUs, the authors report substantial end-to-end inference speedups with little or no retraining cost. The contribution connects learned sparsity to an implementation that can realize its computational value.
icml-2020-inducing-and-exploiting-activa.tldr: Regularization, thresholded activations, and sparse-input convolution jointly enable faster CNN inference while preserving accuracy in most tested architectures.

paragraphs: The paper develops block coordinate optimization methods for composite objectives that can be both non-convex and non-smooth. These methods update groups of variables and incorporate inertia, using information from earlier motion to influence subsequent steps. The aim is to combine flexible block updates with accelerated optimization behavior.

A distinctive feature is the use of two extrapolation points: one for evaluating gradients and another for adding the inertial contribution. The authors empirically find this more efficient than using one point. Their methods also allow random selection of the variable block to update and do not require a restart step.

The theoretical guarantees distinguish between levels of convergence. Subsequential convergence holds under mild assumptions, while convergence of the full sequence requires additional assumptions; the paper also provides rates. These are convergence claims, not a claim of finding a global optimum in every non-convex problem. Experiments on non-negative matrix factorization show favorable competition with existing methods, and further experiments address non-negative tensor factorization.
icml-2020-inertial-block-proximal-method.tldr: Inertial block proximal methods use separate extrapolation points and flexible block selection, with conditional convergence guarantees and favorable factorization experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks when approximately linear features make action selection easier. Earlier work showed that a learner may need to inspect almost every action despite a small uniform approximation error. The authors prove a complementary result: checking only a few actions can always find one whose suboptimality is at most O(epsilon times the square root of d), where d is feature dimension.

This guarantee explains why approximation quality must be assessed together with dimensionality. The authors extend the idea to stochastic bandits, proving a regret bound that combines a learning term with an accumulated feature-approximation term. The bounds do not depend on finer details of the features, although the paper also investigates how feature structure changes the tradeoff between sampling and estimation error.

For reinforcement learning, the result assumes access to a generative model and features that approximate every policy's action-value function within epsilon. Approximate policy iteration then achieves additive error of order epsilon times square root of d divided by (1 − gamma) squared, with a stated sample bound. The assumptions make clear which kind of representation quality supports the guarantee.
icml-2020-learning-with-good-feature-rep.tldr: Approximately linear features can support efficient action selection and reinforcement learning, with guarantees that explicitly trade approximation error against feature dimension.

paragraphs: The paper studies how variational inference shapes the generative model learned by a variational autoencoder. Its focus is the regularization caused by the chosen family of approximate posterior distributions. This asks how an inference choice influences learning itself, beyond its role in approximating a posterior for an already fixed model.

The authors analyze two effects. First, the variational family restricts the set of optimal generative models, helping impart uniqueness to the learned model. Second, it regularizes the decoder's local geometry. This second analysis reveals a regularizer implicit in the beta-VAE objective and leads to an approximate deterministic autoencoding objective with explicit regularizers depending on the decoder's Hessian or Jacobian.

The approximation connects beta-VAEs with heuristics for training regularized autoencoders by expressing related effects through decoder derivatives. Empirical tests find that the deterministic objective behaves similarly to the beta-VAE in objective value and sample quality. The result supports this interpretation of implicit regularization, while the stated relationship remains an approximation rather than an exact equivalence in every setting.
icml-2020-on-implicit-regularization-in-.tldr: The paper explains how variational families regularize beta-VAEs and derives a deterministic approximation with decoder-dependent regularizers and similar empirical behavior.

paragraphs: Dense subgraph discovery seeks a dense component of an edge-weighted graph. Many methods assume that individual edge weights are readily available, but the paper argues that this information may be difficult to obtain. It introduces a learning setting in which observations provide aggregate, noisy information about edges.

The learner queries a subset of edges and receives a noisy sum of their weights. This changes the information available for finding a dense component: the learner works with combined measurements rather than requiring direct access to each weight. For this setting, the authors propose a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a nearly optimal solution with high probability.

The paper also develops a more scalable algorithm for larger graphs and gives it a theoretical guarantee. Experiments on real-world graphs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. The contribution combines a different observation model with algorithms designed for it, showing that useful dense-subgraph discovery is possible under the stated aggregate-feedback setting without assuming easy access to individual edge weights.
icml-2020-online-dense-subgraph-discover.tldr: The paper introduces dense-subgraph discovery from noisy sums of queried edge weights and provides efficient algorithms with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes randomized algorithms for overdetermined least-squares problems. These first-order methods modify gradient steps using an approximate Hessian constructed from a smaller representation, or sketch, of the data matrix. The analysis focuses on Gaussian projections and subsampled randomized Hadamard transforms, abbreviated SRHT.

The main technical result derives the limiting spectral density of SRHT embeddings. The authors use that density and its associated orthogonal polynomials to identify an optimal preconditioned first-order method within the analyzed setting and determine its convergence rate. A parallel analysis uses established random matrix results for Gaussian embeddings. For a fixed sketch size, the SRHT-based method has a faster convergence rate.

The authors then optimize over sketch dimension to develop a new algorithm with improved computational complexity. They describe its complexity as the best known, to their knowledge, among least-squares results without condition-number dependence. The contribution links detailed spectral analysis to algorithm design, addressing both how quickly iterations converge and how the sketch size affects the overall computational cost.
icml-2020-optimal-randomized-first-order.tldr: Spectral analysis yields optimal methods within a class of sketched least-squares solvers and shows faster convergence for SRHT than Gaussian sketches of equal size.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization trains a model against the worst-case risk among distributions near the empirical data distribution. A Wasserstein ball specifies that neighborhood. The paper addresses the theoretical basis for approximating this local worst-case objective, particularly whether the resulting learning method has risk-consistency guarantees.

The authors introduce a minimizer based on a new approximation theorem and establish corresponding risk-consistency results. This strengthens the theoretical justification relative to an earlier tractable approximation whose risk consistency had not been shown. The contribution concerns both the approximation used to make the objective manageable and guarantees for the method derived from it.

The framework also handles locally perturbed training data, with Mixup included as a special case. The approximation and consistency results extend to this setting. Image-classification experiments demonstrate robustness and report significantly higher accuracy than baseline models on noisy datasets. Together, the theory and experiments connect a principled robust objective with a learning procedure that can accommodate local data perturbations.
icml-2020-principled-learning-method-for.tldr: A new approximation supports risk-consistent Wasserstein robust learning, extends to local perturbations including Mixup, and improves accuracy on evaluated noisy datasets.

paragraphs: Shapley-value explanations treat a model's input features as participants in a cooperative game and distribute influence among them. Their appeal rests partly on the mathematical properties of Shapley values and partly on the claim that the resulting allocations serve useful explanatory purposes. This paper examines both justifications.

The authors show that mathematical problems arise when Shapley values are used as feature-importance measures. They argue that attempts to resolve these problems necessarily introduce further complexity, including a need for causal reasoning. The issue is therefore not settled merely by selecting a mathematically distinguished allocation rule: using that rule for feature importance creates additional questions that must be addressed.

The paper also draws on other literature to argue that these allocations do not supply explanations suited to human-centered goals. This separates the properties of an influence score from the purpose an explanation is meant to serve. The contribution is a critique of the justification for Shapley-based feature importance, covering both its mathematical formulation and its suitability for human explanatory needs.
icml-2020-problems-with-shapley-value-ba.tldr: The paper identifies mathematical problems in Shapley-based feature importance and argues that its allocations do not meet human-centered explanation goals.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a mathematical conjecture connected to how stochastic optimization samples data. The motivating question is whether sampling without replacement, also called random reshuffling, converges faster than sampling with replacement. A proposed route to answering this question uses a matrix analogue of the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality.

In the conjectured inequality, positive definite matrices take the place of positive numbers. If the inequality held for every number of matrices, it would imply an advantage for random reshuffling in some important optimization problems. Earlier results had established it for two matrices and a special case involving three. This paper shows that the general conjecture is false.

The proof uses the noncommutative Positivstellensatz to translate the conjecture into a semidefinite program and requirements on its optimum. The authors show that the required bounds fail already at five matrices. This rules out the conjectured inequality as a general justification for the sampling advantage; it does not establish that random reshuffling can never outperform sampling with replacement.
icml-2020-recht-re-noncommutative-arithm.tldr: The paper disproves the general Recht–Ré matrix inequality, invalidating a proposed universal route to proving advantages for random reshuffling.

paragraphs: Post hoc explanations summarize how an already trained black-box model behaves. The paper addresses a weakness of existing explanation methods: their summaries can be unstable or fail under distribution shifts. It proposes using adversarial training to make explanations more robust while keeping them faithful to the model.

The framework optimizes a minimax objective. It seeks an explanation with the best fidelity under the worst perturbation in a specified adversarial set. This builds robustness directly into explanation construction. The authors instantiate the framework for linear explanations and decision sets, developing the optimization procedures needed for both forms.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show substantial improvements in explanation robustness without sacrificing fidelity on the original data distribution. The result concerns the explanation's ability to continue representing the black box under the considered perturbations. The authors also position the framework as, to their knowledge, the first attempt to construct post hoc explanations robust to a general class of practically relevant adversarial perturbations.
icml-2020-robust-and-stable-black-box-ex.tldr: Adversarially trained explanations improve robustness in experiments while preserving fidelity to the black-box model on the original data distribution.

paragraphs: The paper proposes separating two kinds of information in a neural network with external memory: individual experiences and relationships among those experiences. Its motivation is that a single memory can provide a lossy account of interactions between stored items. Separate item and relational memories are intended to support richer relationship representations.

The Self-attentive Associative Memory operator, or SAM, constructs relational memory from item memory. Based on an outer-product operation, it forms associative memories representing hypothetical higher-order relationships between arbitrary pairs of memory elements. The two memories are then connected within one sequential model, giving the system mechanisms for both retaining items and reasoning about their relationships.

The authors evaluate the model across synthetic problems and practical tasks involving geometry, graphs, reinforcement learning, and question answering. They report competitive results across this range. The contribution is an explicit architectural treatment of stored experiences and their relationships, with empirical evidence that the combined model can support both memorization and relational reasoning in diverse tasks.
icml-2020-self-attentive-associative-mem.tldr: SAM connects separate item and relational memories to support memorization and relationship reasoning, with competitive results across diverse tasks.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning creates training labels from the inputs themselves. This paper shows how that idea can improve accuracy even when human-provided labels are already available for the full dataset. The method combines the original prediction task with a self-supervised task through an augmented label space.

Instead of adding separate task losses, the model learns one unified task defined over the joint distribution of original and self-supervised labels. The authors explain that this relaxes an invariance constraint that arises when learning the two tasks simultaneously, making training easier. At inference time, predictions from different input augmentations can also be aggregated to improve accuracy.

The paper then introduces self-distillation to transfer the effect of that aggregated inference into a single, faster inference. This addresses the prediction-time cost of combining multiple augmentations. Experiments report large accuracy improvements across fully supervised settings, including few-shot and imbalanced classification. The contribution combines a different way to formulate training labels with techniques for improving predictions and retaining those benefits more efficiently.
icml-2020-self-supervised-label-augmenta.tldr: Joint original and self-supervised labels improve supervised learning, while aggregated predictions and self-distillation extend the accuracy benefits to inference.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks must allocate a limited parameter budget across layers. The paper argues that uniform allocations and heuristic non-uniform allocations can leave accuracy or computational efficiency on the table. It proposes learning that allocation through Soft Threshold Reparameterization, abbreviated STR.

STR applies a soft-threshold operator to network weights and learns the pruning thresholds as sparsity develops. This produces a non-uniform sparsity budget through training. On ResNet50 and MobileNetV1 evaluated on ImageNet-1K, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy for unstructured sparsity. The learned budgets also empirically reduce floating-point operation counts by up to 50%.

In the 99% sparsity regime, STR improves accuracy over existing results by up to 10%, according to the reported evaluation. The method can also induce low-rank structure in recurrent neural networks, extending its use beyond unstructured CNN pruning. These findings support learned thresholds as a simple way to decide where parameters should remain, with benefits for both prediction accuracy and arithmetic cost in the tested settings.
icml-2020-soft-threshold-weight-reparame.tldr: STR learns pruning thresholds and layer-wise sparsity budgets, improving reported sparse-network accuracy and reducing FLOPs by up to 50%.

paragraphs: Backpropagation's biological plausibility is challenged by weight transport: the requirement that a neuron access another neuron's synaptic weights. This paper investigates learning rules that avoid instantaneous weight transport while still supporting large-scale learning. It considers both local rules and non-local mechanisms based on estimating weights.

The authors first examine a recently proposed local rule with competitive performance and find that it depends heavily on tuning choices that do not transfer across architectures. Their analysis identifies a mathematical source of instability and leads to a more robust local rule with better transfer without retuning. Nevertheless, a performance and stability gap relative to backpropagation remains and grows as networks become deeper.

The second route uses non-local rules that replace instantaneous transport with weight estimation. These rules match state-of-the-art deep-network performance in the reported experiments and tolerate noisy updates. The findings suggest two research directions: making local rules reliable across architectures and finding biological implementations of non-local learning. They do not establish that the proposed mechanisms are implemented by biological neural systems.
icml-2020-two-routes-to-scalable-credit-.tldr: The paper improves local learning without weight symmetry and finds that non-local weight-estimation rules can match strong deep-network performance.

paragraphs: The paper studies adaptation when data distributions change gradually over time. A classifier starts with training on a source domain and then receives only unlabeled data along a path toward a target domain. The goal is to use this sequence of intermediate distributions to handle a larger overall shift.

The authors prove a non-vacuous upper bound on self-training error under gradual shifts. Their analysis includes settings in which adapting directly to the target can produce unbounded error. The result shows how access to a gradual sequence can change what is theoretically achievable, rather than treating the source and target as the only distributions available.

The theory also highlights regularization and label sharpening as essential in the analyzed setting, even with infinite data. Thus, additional data alone does not remove the need for these algorithmic choices. Experiments on rotating MNIST, forest Cover Type, and Portraits show higher accuracy when the method uses the gradual-shift structure. The contribution combines an error guarantee with practical guidance for adaptation along an evolving distribution.
icml-2020-understanding-self-training-fo.tldr: Gradual self-training receives an informative error guarantee and improves adaptation accuracy by using intermediate distributions, regularization, and label sharpening.
